claims.claim: The four inner planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars — are the terrestrial planets: rocky worlds with solid surfaces, made mostly of rock and metal, in contrast to the giant planets beyond them, which lack hard surfaces.

The terrestrial planets are small compared with the giant planets and share a layered structure of dense metal core, rocky mantle, and solid crust; Earth, Venus, and Mars have broadly similar bulk compositions, roughly one-third iron-bearing metal and two-thirds silicates.

Mercury is the smallest terrestrial planet (diameter about 4,880 km), orbits at about 0.4 AU, has a heavily cratered surface and essentially no atmosphere, and its surface temperature swings from about 430 C in daylight to about -180 C at night; it is not the hottest planet.

Venus is nearly Earth's size (diameter about 12,104 km vs Earth's 12,756 km), orbits at about 0.72 AU, and is the hottest planet in the solar system: its thick, mostly carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, giving a surface temperature of about 467 C and surface pressure about 93 times Earth's sea-level pressure; its day (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 Earth days), and it spins backward relative to Earth.

Earth is the largest terrestrial planet (diameter about 12,756 km), the only planet in our solar system known to have liquid water on its surface (oceans cover about 71 percent), with an atmosphere of about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen, and the only known world to host life, which began here about 3.8 billion years ago.

Mars is about half Earth's diameter (about 6,780 km), orbits at about 1.52 AU, and has a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide; it hosts the largest volcano (Olympus Mons, more than 40 km tall) and the largest canyon (Valles Marineris, about 3,870 km long) in the solar system, polar ice caps, and evidence of past liquid water in ancient river valleys, deltas, and lakebeds.

Comparative planetology: Venus, Earth, and Mars started from similar rocky material yet evolved differently — Venus became hot and dry through a runaway greenhouse effect, Mars became cold and dry as its thin atmosphere lets heat escape (sometimes called a runaway refrigerator effect), and only Earth kept a hospitable climate.

Earth is the only known planet to host life; the general conditions that support life here include temperatures that keep liquid water stable at the surface, a protective atmosphere that shields the surface from much harmful radiation, and a hospitable mix of chemicals.

The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth's average surface temperature near 15 C, more than 30 C warmer than it would be without an atmosphere; a balanced greenhouse, rather than a runaway one, is part of why Earth is habitable.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft (public/content/phase-3/lessons.json entry for this topic) contains only boilerplate ('Terrestrial Planets is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science...') with no factual content beyond the topic name; it was discarded and the lesson written fresh from verified sources.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate draft entirely with original, source-verified prose.
Used NASA's current figures: Venus surface about 467 C, Valles Marineris about 3,870 km, Mercury day/night about 430 C / -180 C.
Explicitly corrected the common misconception that Mercury, being closest to the Sun, is the hottest planet — Venus is, because of its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere.
Corrected the assumption that all terrestrial planets have thick atmospheres: only Venus does; Mercury is nearly airless and Mars's atmosphere is thin.
Kept the 'evidence of past water on Mars' claim separate from any claim about past life: flowing water is evidence of water, not of life.
rightsIssues: NASA Science pages are U.S. government works; used reference-only with fully original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Composition and Structure of Planets (Astronomy 2e, section 7.2)
sourceRecords.notes: openstax.org book pages render via JavaScript and do not serve text to direct fetches, and no Wayback capture exists; the section text was therefore read from the official OpenStax source repository (github.com/openstax/osbooks-astronomy, module m59819 'Composition and Structure of Planets'). Supports: two distinct families of planets; terrestrial planets are much smaller than the giants and composed primarily of rocks (silicates of silicon and oxygen) and metals (chiefly iron); Earth, Venus, and Mars have roughly similar bulk compositions of about one-third iron-nickel or iron-sulfur combinations and two-thirds silicates; densest metals sit in a central core with lighter silicates near the surface. Facts synthesized; no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Mercury (Astronomy 2e, section 9.2)
sourceRecords.notes: Read from the official OpenStax source repository (module m59835 'Mercury') because the openstax.org web pages are JavaScript-rendered. Supports: Mercury is similar to the Moon in having no appreciable atmosphere and a heavily cratered surface; surface temperature climbs to 700 K (430 C) at noontime and drops to about 100 K (-170 C) just before dawn. Facts synthesized; no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Massive Atmosphere of Venus (Astronomy 2e, section 10.3)
sourceRecords.notes: Read from the official OpenStax source repository (module m59840 'The Massive Atmosphere of Venus'). Supports: carbon dioxide is the most abundant gas on Venus, about 96 percent of the atmosphere; surface pressure about 90 bars; the runaway greenhouse effect as an evolutionary process in which extra heat increases atmospheric CO2 and water vapor, amplifying warming until a new, much hotter equilibrium is reached. Facts synthesized; no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Divergent Planetary Evolution (Astronomy 2e, section 10.6)
sourceRecords.notes: Read from the official OpenStax source repository (module m59847 'Divergent Planetary Evolution'). Supports: Venus, Mars, and Earth orbit in roughly the same inner zone and apparently started with about the same chemical mix of silicates and metals, yet their evolutionary paths diverged — Venus became hot and dry, Mars became cold and dry, and only Earth ended up with a climate we consider hospitable; the runaway greenhouse effect on Venus and the runaway refrigerator effect on Mars are named as the mechanisms, with the exact triggers not fully understood. Facts synthesized; no source wording reproduced.
